title: Active recon: touching the target
description: Host discovery, service enumeration, version detection.

1.title: Host discovery
1.body:
## The first sweep

Before scanning ports, you need to know WHO is alive in the range:

```bash
# Nmap ping sweep (ICMP + ARP on local networks)
nmap -sn 10.10.10.0/24           # -sn = no port scan, discovery only
nmap -sn -PR 10.10.10.0/24       # ARP only (local networks: the most reliable)

# Classic alternatives
fping -asg 10.10.10.0/24         # fast and quiet
arp-scan --localnet              # pure ARP: finds what blocks ICMP
```

## Why ARP > ICMP on local networks

A well-configured firewall blocks (inbound) ICMP ping. But **ARP** is required
for the network to work: if the machine doesn't answer ARP, it can't communicate. That's why
`arp-scan` on the same subnet finds EVERYTHING that is powered on, even "hidden" hosts.

On remote (non-local) networks, ARP doesn't get through — ICMP, TCP SYN to common ports
(80, 443) and UDP are used instead. Nmap combines techniques with `-sn` by default.

## The expected result

A list of live IPs. Each one is a target for the port scan in the next task.
In an internal network pentest, this sweep can uncover forgotten machines (the
printer with open FTP, the lab Raspberry Pi, the Windows Server 2003 that
nobody patches).

> **Noise**: a ping sweep of a /24 is VERY visible in any SIEM. In engagements with
> stealth rules, the window and technique are agreed with the client.

recon-activo-escaneo-t01-q01.prompt: What tool sends ICMP pings to a range?

recon-activo-escaneo-t01-q02.prompt: What layer-2 protocol discovers hosts even with ICMP firewall?
recon-activo-escaneo-t01-q02.hint: You already met it in the cmd room: arp -a

recon-activo-escaneo-t01-q03.prompt: A host responds to ARP but not ping. Is it alive?
recon-activo-escaneo-t01-q03.hint: ARP is layer 2: if it answers, the interface exists.

options.a: No: ping is the only indicator
options.b: Yes: the ARP reply proves the machine is powered on and connected (it only blocks ICMP)
options.c: Only if it also answers HTTP

2.title: Port scanning
2.body:
## Anatomy of a scan

The most common port scan (**SYN scan**, `-sS` in Nmap):

```text
Scanner          →  SYN    →  Port 22        (are you open?)
Scanner  ←  SYN-ACK  ←      Port 22        (yes, open)
Scanner          →  RST    →  Port 22        (thanks, leaving without connecting)
```

It never completes the handshake → the service does NOT record it in its application logs
(although the firewall may see it). It's fast and semi-stealthy.

The THREE states that matter:

| State | Meaning | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **open** | something is listening there | enumerate the version |
| **closed** | the machine answers RST: nobody is listening | move on |
| **filtered** | a firewall/IDS swallows the packet | an interesting port all the same |

```bash
nmap -sS -p- 10.10.10.5        # SYN scan of ALL ports (65535)
nmap -sS --top-ports 100 10.10.10.5   # the 100 most common (fast)
```

## TCP connect scan vs SYN scan

- `-sT` (connect): completes the handshake. Slower, more noise in the app logs.
- `-sS` (SYN): the classic — it requires root but it's the pentester's standard.

## UDP (the unfinished business)

UDP has no handshake: scanning it is slow and ambiguous (was the packet lost or is the port
open?). `nmap -sU --top-ports 50` covers DNS(53), SNMP(161), DHCP(67). A forgotten UDP
service (SNMP with the `public` community) is pure gold on corporate networks.

recon-activo-escaneo-t02-q01.prompt: What does a SYN (half-open) scan send, and what does it do when it receives a SYN-ACK?
recon-activo-escaneo-t02-q01.hint: It's called half-open for a reason: it never finishes the handshake.

options.a: It sends SYN and, on receiving SYN-ACK, completes the handshake with an ACK
options.b: It sends SYN and, on receiving SYN-ACK, replies RST without completing the connection
options.c: It sends FIN and, on receiving SYN-ACK, marks the port as filtered
options.d: It sends ACK and, on receiving SYN-ACK, repeats the probe over UDP

recon-activo-escaneo-t02-q02.prompt: What are the three main port states?

recon-activo-escaneo-t02-q03.prompt: What state indicates a firewall blocking?
recon-activo-escaneo-t02-q03.hint: You don't know whether it's open: something is swallowing the packet.

3.title: Versions
3.body:
## The flag that changes everything: -sV

```bash
nmap -sV -sS -p 22,80,443,445 10.10.10.5
```

Without `-sV`, Nmap says "port 80 open". With `-sV`:

```text
PORT   STATE SERVICE VERSION
22/tcp open  ssh     OpenSSH 8.2p1 Ubuntu 4ubuntu0.3
80/tcp open  http    Apache httpd 2.4.49 ((Unix))
443/tcp open  ssl/https Apache httpd 2.4.49
445/tcp open  netbios-ssn Samba smbd 4.6.2
```

**That output is the input for the exploit**: exact version → searchsploit → CVE.

## OS detection and NSE scripts

```bash
nmap -O 10.10.10.5              # guesses the OS from the TCP/IP stack
nmap -sV --script=banner 10.10.10.5    # grabs the services' banners
nmap --script vuln 10.10.10.5    # scripts for known vulnerabilities (noisy!)
```

**NSE scripts** (Nmap Scripting Engine) are the heavy artillery: from detecting
EternalBlue (`smb-vuln-ms17-010`) to enumerating SMB users
(`smb-enum-users.nse`). There are 600+ official ones: `ls /usr/share/nmap/scripts/`.

## The complete professional workflow (memorize it)

```bash
# 1. Who is alive
nmap -sn 10.10.10.0/24
# 2. Which ports (fast scan first)
nmap -sS --top-ports 100 -oA scan_rapido <vivos>
# 3. All ports on the interesting hosts
nmap -sS -p- -oA scan_completo <objetivo>
# 4. Versions + scripts on the open ports
nmap -sV -sC -p <abiertos> -oA scan_versiones <objetivo>
# 5. searchsploit <version> → exploit
```

`-oA` saves in three formats (normal, grepable, XML) for later processing. `-sC`
runs the "default" scripts (safe and useful).

With this workflow you can enumerate any network in minutes. The next module (Nmap
Pro) takes it to a professional level, and after that Burp Suite does the same for
web applications.

recon-activo-escaneo-t03-q01.prompt: What Nmap flag detects service version?

recon-activo-escaneo-t03-q02.prompt: Which Nmap NSE script reads the welcome message each service sends on connect (which often reveals the software and its version)?
recon-activo-escaneo-t03-q02.hint: The script is named after that welcome message.

recon-activo-escaneo-t03-q03.prompt: You see Apache 2.4.49. What is your NEXT action?

options.a: Ignore port 80: it's just a website
options.b: searchsploit apache 2.4.49 and check whether the CVE applies (path traversal + RCE)
options.c: Close nmap and write the report

4.title: Lab: DNS enumeration and zone transfer
4.body:
## DNS as a map (which they sometimes hand you whole)

A target's DNS enumerates its infrastructure: subdomains, mail servers,
nameservers, and sometimes — internal hosts nobody intended to publish. The
lab simulates a `dig` and an AXFR:

```bash
cd labs/dns-enumerate && cp flags.env.example flags.env
docker compose --env-file flags.env up -d

# Normal queries (what anyone can see):
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18098/dig?name=victima.com" | jq .
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18098/dig?name=www.victima.com" | jq .
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18098/dig?name=vpn.victima.com" | jq .   # NXDOMAIN?

# The real dig equivalent:
# dig victima.com ANY && dig vpn.victima.com
```

## Zone transfer (AXFR): the full dump

AXFR is the REPLICATION mechanism between nameservers: it transfers the
ENTIRE zone (every record). A misconfigured NS allows it for
any client:

```bash
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18098/axfr?server=ns1.victima.com" | jq .

# In real life:
# dig @ns1.victima.com victima.com AXFR
```

Notice what the dump reveals that normal queries do NOT: internal
hosts (vpn, staging, intranet), IP addresses from private segments
and "forgotten" records. It's the classic OSINT/active finding: zero
exploitation, maximum map.

## Subdomain hunting (beyond the lab)

| Technique | Tool |
|---|---|
| Open AXFR | `dig @ns AXFR` (increasingly rare, but it still happens) |
| Subdomain brute force | `gobuster dns -d dominio -w wordlist.txt` |
| Certificate Transparency | crt.sh — certificates reveal hosts |
| Passive DNS | SecurityTrails, VirusTotal |

**Defense**: restrict AXFR to the IPs of the slave NSs
(`allow-transfer { slaves; };` in BIND), and separate the internal DNS from the
external one (split-horizon): .int hosts must not live in the public zone
NOR on the same server that serves it.

recon-activo-escaneo-t04-q01.prompt: Query /dig for vpn.victima.com. What IP does it answer? (x.x.x.x format)
recon-activo-escaneo-t04-q01.hint: curl 'http://127.0.0.1:18098/dig?name=vpn.victima.com' — the real-world equivalent: dig vpn.victima.com

recon-activo-escaneo-t04-q02.prompt: The nameservers allow AXFR to anyone. Dump the zone and submit the flag annotated on the staging record.
recon-activo-escaneo-t04-q02.hint: curl 'http://127.0.0.1:18098/axfr?server=ns1.victima.com' — in real life: dig @ns1.victima.com victima.com AXFR

recon-activo-escaneo-t04-q03.prompt: The dump lists hosts you did not know about (including a secret admin panel). Query the internal environment record (internal.victima.com) and submit its flag.
recon-activo-escaneo-t04-q03.hint: curl 'http://127.0.0.1:18098/dig?name=internal.victima.com' — the name is discovered IN the AXFR listing
